content: Who has believed our message? To whom has the LORD’s arm been revealed? {{v:2}} For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. {{v:3}} He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. {{v:4}} Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. {{v:5}} But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. {{v:6}} All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. {{v:7}} He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth. {{v:8}} He was taken away by oppression and judgment. As for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people? {{v:9}} They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, nor was any deceit in his mouth. {{v:10}} Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he will see his offspring. He will prolong his days and the LORD’s pleasure will prosper in his hand. {{v:11}} After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. {{v:12}} Therefore I will give him a portion with the great. He will divide the plunder with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

facets.text: The Suffering Servant's affliction is not the tragedy it appears to be but a vicarious, substitutionary bearing of guilt: he is "pierced for our transgressions" and "crushed for our iniquities," and it is by his wounds that we are healed. The passage reframes what onlookers first misjudged as divine punishment for the Servant's own sin into the redemptive suffering he endures on behalf of others. This is the clearest Old Testament articulation of atonement through innocent, representative suffering.
facets.question: How can one person's suffering take away the sins of others?

facets.text: The universality of human sin is confessed in the image of a scattered, self-willed flock: "All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way." Against this collective straying, the LORD deliberately lays "the iniquity of us all" on the one Servant, so that human waywardness meets its remedy not in human effort but in a burden divinely transferred. The passage thus binds together universal guilt and a single point of atonement.
facets.question: Why does Scripture say everyone has gone astray, and how is that condition remedied?

facets.text: Catholic tradition reads this Servant as a direct prophecy of Jesus Christ, whose passion fulfills every detail: silent before his accusers, numbered with criminals, buried in a rich man's tomb, yet innocent of violence or deceit. The Gospels and Acts explicitly cite this chapter of Christ, and the Church proclaims it in the Good Friday liturgy. Isaiah 53 is the paschal mystery written in prophecy centuries before Calvary.
facets.question: How does Isaiah 53 point to and describe the passion of Jesus Christ?

facets.text: The Servant is portrayed as the true sacrificial Lamb: "as a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn't open his mouth." His silence is not weakness but the willing self-offering of a sin offering, fulfilling and surpassing the temple sacrifices. This lamb imagery is taken up in John the Baptist's cry, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world."
facets.question: Why is the Suffering Servant described as a silent lamb led to slaughter?

facets.text: The passage moves beyond death to vindication and fruitfulness: after making his soul "an offering for sin" the Servant will "see his offspring," "prolong his days," and "see the light and be satisfied." This foreshadows the resurrection, in which the crucified Servant is not annihilated but glorified, and his self-offering bears an abundant spiritual harvest. Redemptive suffering is thus crowned with life, not defeat.
facets.question: Does the Suffering Servant's death lead to resurrection and new life?

facets.text: The Servant justifies "many" not by external decree alone but "by the knowledge of himself," bearing their iniquities so that righteousness is communicated to them. This anticipates the Catholic understanding of justification as a real sharing in Christ's righteousness through knowing and being united to him. The one righteous Servant becomes the source of righteousness for the multitude.
facets.question: What does it mean that the righteous Servant justifies many by knowledge of himself?

facets.text: The chapter opens with a lament over unbelief: "Who has believed our message? To whom has the LORD's arm been revealed?" The saving work of God is hidden in lowliness — a Servant with "no beauty that we should desire him" — and can only be recognized through the gift of faith. God's power is revealed precisely where human eyes see only weakness and rejection.
facets.question: Why is God's saving power hidden in weakness and often not believed?

facets.text: The Servant's redemptive work culminates in ongoing intercession: "he poured out his soul to death... yet he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors." His self-emptying to death is inseparable from his priestly pleading for sinners, prefiguring Christ the eternal High Priest who ever lives to intercede. Atonement here is not merely a past transaction but a continuing priestly mediation.
facets.question: How does the Suffering Servant intercede as a priest for sinners?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Isaiah 53, the fourth Servant Song, prophesies a despised, innocent Servant whose vicarious suffering atones for the sins of all, culminating in his vindication, justification of many, and priestly intercession — read by the Church as prophecy of Christ's passion and resurrection.

[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The Servant is pierced and crushed for our transgressions, bearing guilt substitutionally so that by his wounds we are healed — the OT foundation of vicarious atonement.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: All have gone astray like sheep, and the LORD lays the iniquity of all on one Servant, binding universal sin to a single point of atonement.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The Church reads the silent, innocent, criminal-numbered, rich-man-buried Servant as prophecy of Christ's passion, cited in the NT and the Good Friday liturgy.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The Servant as silent lamb led to slaughter is the true sin offering surpassing temple sacrifice, fulfilled in the Lamb of God who takes away the world's sin.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: After offering his soul for sin, the Servant sees offspring, prolongs his days, and sees the light — foreshadowing resurrection and the fruitfulness of redemptive suffering.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: The righteous Servant justifies many by knowledge of himself and bears their iniquities, anticipating justification as a real sharing in Christ's righteousness.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: The opening lament over unbelief shows God's saving power hidden in a Servant without beauty, recognized only through faith.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The Servant pours out his soul to death yet bears many sins and intercedes for transgressors, prefiguring Christ the eternal High Priest's continuing mediation.
